q: A shop predicts next month’s sales amount. Which technique fits?
why: Regression predicts a numeric value. Classification predicts categories; clustering groups similar records.

clues.why: The output is a number, rather than a category.

hint: Name the type of output before choosing a technique.
analysis: The task is forecasting a numeric sales value. Select a numeric prediction technique; the business being a shop is background.
trap: Do not choose classification merely because sales records contain categories.
reasons: Classification predicts a class, such as high or low sales, rather than the requested amount.
Regression predicts a continuous numeric target, such as sales revenue.
Clustering discovers groups; it does not directly predict a future sales amount.
Translation converts languages and does not solve numeric forecasting.

q: A model learns from emails already marked spam or safe. What is this?
why: Supervised learning uses labeled examples. The spam labels supply the target answers.

clues.why: Known target labels are available during training.

hint: Ask whether the desired answers are supplied with the examples.
analysis: The key condition is that training emails already have spam/safe labels. That is different from discovering groups without labels.
trap: Spam is the application; labeled examples determine the learning type.
reasons: Unsupervised learning discovers structure without target labels.
Reinforcement learning uses feedback about actions and rewards, not just labeled email examples.
Supervised learning maps examples to known target labels.
Pre-training describes a training stage, not the best description of these labeled examples.

q: Which metric matters most when missing actual fraud is especially costly?
why: Recall measures the proportion of actual fraud cases detected, directly addressing missed positives.

clues.why: False negatives are the error the business most wants to reduce.

hint: Focus on the costliest error, not a generic overall score.
analysis: Find the priority: catching actual fraud. Recall measures detected positives out of all actual positives.
trap: High accuracy can hide missed fraud when most transactions are legitimate.
reasons: Recall measures the proportion of actual fraud cases detected, directly addressing missed positives.
Precision measures how trustworthy positive fraud alerts are, rather than how many actual fraud cases were missed.
Accuracy can be dominated by legitimate transactions when fraud is rare.
F1 balances precision and recall; the stated priority specifically emphasizes missed fraud and therefore recall.

q: Which AWS service converts recorded speech into text?
why: Transcribe recognizes speech. Polly does the reverse: text to speech.

clues.why: Check the direction of conversion.

hint: Identify what goes in and what must come out.
analysis: Audio is the input and a transcript is the output. Choose speech recognition rather than speech synthesis.
trap: Polly and Transcribe are easy to reverse: read the input/output direction.
reasons: Polly generates speech from text, the reverse direction.
Translate converts text between languages.
Comprehend analyzes text; it does not transcribe audio.
Transcribe converts speech recordings into text.

q: Which TWO tasks should primarily use deterministic rules rather than a probabilistic model?
options: Group customers by similar purchasing behavior
Calculate a tax amount using an exact published formula
Enforce whether an identity has permission to read a restricted object
reasons: Grouping by similarity can use ML clustering.
An exact formula should be computed directly rather than estimated.
Object recognition is a common computer-vision task.
Authorization must be enforced by a policy decision, not guessed by a model.
Forecasting unknown future values is a common prediction task.
why: Exact formulas and permission enforcement require rule-based outcomes, while clustering, vision and forecasting can benefit from learned predictions.

clues.why: Choose tasks requiring exact calculation or an enforced access decision.

hint: Look for exact outcomes, and select exactly two tasks.
analysis: Distinguish uncertain prediction from actions that must follow exact rules. Both the calculation and the authorization condition need deterministic enforcement.
trap: A model may help describe a rule, but it should not replace the calculation or authorization control.

q: What is a token in a language model?
options: A unit of text processed by the model
Exactly one complete word in every case
Exactly one character in every case
The entire prompt treated as one indivisible item
why: A token is a model-processing unit; a tokenizer can represent words, word fragments or other text units.

clues.why: The question asks about model text processing, not account security.

hint: Think about the pieces into which model input is split.
analysis: Interpret token in the language-model context. It refers to text units; the same word can mean credentials in other contexts.
trap: A familiar security meaning of token is a distractor here.
reasons: A token is a model-processing unit; a tokenizer can represent words, word fragments or other text units.
One word can use multiple tokens; the correspondence is not always one token per word.
Tokens are not necessarily single characters, although some may represent a character.
A prompt typically consists of many tokens, not one indivisible unit.

q: What does an embedding represent?
options: An encrypted copy of the source text
A numeric representation of semantic features
The position of a word in a billing record
A confidence score proving an answer is factual
why: Embeddings encode features in numeric vectors used in tasks such as semantic similarity search.

clues.why: The concept represents semantic information numerically.

hint: Look for a representation that enables similarity comparison.
analysis: Identify what embeddings do: encode features in vectors, allowing related content to be compared.
trap: A vector is a representation, not encryption or a guarantee of meaning.
reasons: Embeddings are representations, not encryption, and should not be treated as protection against data disclosure.
Embeddings encode features in numeric vectors used in tasks such as semantic similarity search.
A billing-record position does not describe semantic vector representation.
A vector embedding does not prove an answer is correct or supply a calibrated factual confidence score.

q: A chatbot invents a believable citation. What is this called?
why: Fabricating a plausible citation is an example of hallucination: generated content without factual support.

clues.why: The output sounds credible but lacks factual support.

hint: Distinguish fluent wording from verified evidence.
analysis: The failure is fabricated factual content. Neither a confident tone nor a citation-shaped string proves truth.
trap: Do not treat a plausible citation as a checked source.
reasons: Data poisoning corrupts training or source data; the scenario describes an unsupported generated assertion.
Prompt injection involves instructions trying to redirect the system; no such attack is described.
Fabricating a plausible citation is an example of hallucination: generated content without factual support.
Distillation trains a smaller model from a teacher and is not the name for fabricated content.

q: Which service offers managed access to foundation models from multiple providers?
why: Bedrock provides managed foundation-model access. S3 stores objects; Config tracks resource configuration.

clues.why: The requirement is managed foundation-model access, not storage.

hint: Choose the service whose main purpose matches the requested capability.
analysis: Match both conditions: managed model access and a choice of providers. Other cloud services may support the application but do not provide this capability.
trap: A component used by an AI app is not necessarily the model-access service.
reasons: CloudTrail provides activity logging for audit use.
S3 stores objects; it does not itself provide managed model inference.
Config tracks resource configuration and compliance rules.
Bedrock offers managed access to foundation models from different providers.

q: Match each AI application concept to its primary role.
reasons: IAM determines what an identity may access or do.
Fine-tuning adapts model weights using training examples.
MCP standardizes connections to external tools and context.
RAG retrieves source material to supply as generation context.
why: MCP connects; IAM authorizes; RAG retrieves grounding material; fine-tuning updates weights.

clues.why: These capabilities solve different parts of the application.

hint: Separate connecting, authorizing, retrieving and training.
analysis: Match each capability to its specific job; do not assume a tool-connection protocol provides permission enforcement.
trap: A connected tool still requires authorization, and retrieved content is not itself model training.
prompts: Standardize connection to external tools and context
Limit an identity to approved actions and resources
Supply current document passages at answer time
Adapt model weights using curated training examples

q: A chatbot needs this week’s internal policies without retraining. Choose an approach.
options: Fine-tune only on last month’s policies
Distill a smaller model from the current model
why: RAG can retrieve current policy passages and supply them as runtime context without changing model weights.

clues.why: The knowledge is changing and must be supplied at answer time.

hint: Separate fresh knowledge from changing the model’s behavior.
analysis: The task requires current internal information with no retraining. Retrieval can supply updated documents as context; verify retrieval freshness and access rights too.
trap: No retraining alone is not a universal RAG rule; it fits here because fresh document knowledge is required.
reasons: RAG can retrieve current policy passages and supply them as runtime context without changing model weights.
Fine-tuning updates weights and last month’s examples do not supply this week’s changes.
Pre-training changes weights and is unnecessary for retrieving frequently changing documents.
Distillation transfers model behavior; it does not itself fetch this week’s private documents.

q: A prompt includes three examples of the desired response. Which technique is used?
why: Few-shot prompting supplies examples in context. It does not update model weights.

clues.why: The prompt demonstrates the desired behavior.

hint: Count examples in the prompt, not model parameters.
analysis: Three demonstrations supplied in the prompt make this few-shot prompting. The model is not being trained on a new dataset.
trap: Examples in a prompt are not automatically fine-tuning.
reasons: Zero-shot prompting does not supply task demonstrations.
Distillation trains a student to learn from a teacher model.
Few-shot prompting uses a small number of examples in context.
Pre-training learns model parameters from a broad training corpus.

q: Which change generally makes model responses less random?
options: Increase top K to admit more candidates
why: Lower temperature generally favors higher-probability tokens and reduces randomness; factual correctness is still not guaranteed.

clues.why: The requested change is about sampling variation.

hint: Match the parameter to the behavior it controls.
analysis: Choose the control for randomness. Lower temperature generally concentrates sampling, but output correctness still requires evaluation.
trap: Less random does not mean more factual in every case.
reasons: An output-token cap controls length rather than directly reducing sampling variation.
Lower temperature generally favors higher-probability tokens and reduces randomness; factual correctness is still not guaranteed.
A higher top K admits more candidate tokens and is not the requested reduction in sampling variation.
Context capacity limits the information that can fit, rather than directly setting sampling randomness.

q: A team wants a smaller model to learn from a larger model’s outputs. What is this?
why: Distillation trains a smaller student to learn from a larger teacher model.

clues.why: A smaller student is learning from a larger teacher.

hint: Distinguish training a student from retrieving documents.
analysis: The goal is transferring capabilities from a larger model to a smaller one. That is a model-training relationship rather than context retrieval.
trap: Do not confuse distillation with compressing a prompt.
reasons: Few-shot prompting supplies examples at inference time without training a student model.
RAG retrieves source material for context and does not itself train a student.
Prompt caching reuses supported processing of repeated context rather than transferring model capabilities.
Distillation trains a smaller student to learn from a larger teacher model.

q: Which outcome best measures a support agent’s business usefulness?
why: Measure task completion against cost and quality goals, rather than model size alone.

clues.why: The measure must reflect a real user outcome.

hint: Ask what success means to the business.
analysis: The task is evaluating a support agent as a product. Successful task completion balanced with cost and quality is more meaningful than size or verbosity.
trap: A larger model or longer answer is not automatically more useful.
reasons: Task completion with acceptable cost connects performance to a business objective.
Long answers may be irrelevant or costly; length alone is not success.
Parameter count is a model characteristic, not a direct business result.
Vector count indicates stored representations, not customer outcomes.

q: A hiring model performs poorly for one demographic. What should the team examine?
options: Rely on the aggregate accuracy alone
Increase inference capacity before evaluating errors
Compare subgroup outcomes and training-data representation
Use only a random sample dominated by the largest group
why: Subgroup evaluation and representation checks help investigate whether the system serves different populations adequately.

clues.why: Overall metrics may conceal subgroup differences.

hint: Look beyond the average score to who experiences errors.
analysis: The concern is uneven performance across groups. Examine subgroup outcomes and representation before deciding what corrective action is justified.
trap: Bias is not ruled out by high aggregate accuracy.
reasons: An overall score can conceal a much higher error rate for a subgroup.
Capacity affects throughput and latency; it does not diagnose demographic prediction disparities.
Subgroup evaluation and representation checks help investigate whether the system serves different populations adequately.
A majority-dominated sample may repeat the blind spot affecting the underrepresented group.

q: What does model explainability help users understand?
options: How to reduce endpoint hosting costs
How to encrypt every training record
Whether every prediction is guaranteed factual
why: Explainability helps people interpret influential factors or reasons behind a model prediction.

clues.why: The user needs an interpretation of the model’s decision.

hint: Separate explanation from access to raw training data.
analysis: The goal is understanding the reasons or influential factors behind a prediction. This does not require exposing confidential training records.
trap: An explanation of influential factors is not a proof of causation.
reasons: Hosting-cost optimization is an operational concern, not what explainability describes.
Explainability helps people interpret influential factors or reasons behind a model prediction.
Encryption protects data; it does not explain a particular prediction.
An explanation is not a guarantee that a prediction is correct or fair.

q: Which feature helps filter harmful content in a Bedrock application?
why: Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable content safeguards, which should be evaluated alongside other controls.

clues.why: The required capability is a generation safeguard.

hint: Choose a control that acts on model input or output.
analysis: Match a content-safety requirement to a configurable safeguard. Keep other controls and evaluation because filtering is imperfect.
trap: Guardrails reduce risk; they are not an absolute safety guarantee.
reasons: Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable content safeguards, which should be evaluated alongside other controls.
IAM controls authorization; it does not itself classify and filter generated harmful text.
CloudTrail supports auditing account activity rather than directly filtering a response.
Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it is not the Bedrock response content-filter feature.

q: What should a team assess before commercial use of generated artwork?
why: Generated content can carry intellectual-property risks. Review rights and intended use before publishing.

clues.why: The intended use raises rights and licensing questions.

hint: Ask what nontechnical risk remains even when generation succeeds.
analysis: The scenario asks what to assess before publication, not how to improve model performance. Rights and intellectual-property risks directly affect commercial reuse.
trap: Being generated by AI does not automatically grant unrestricted rights.
reasons: Dimensions affect presentation, not permission to use the artwork.
Rendering speed affects efficiency, not licensing or ownership risk.
Token count is not evidence of intellectual-property clearance.
Usage rights and IP risks should be assessed for the intended use.

q: Which approach best supports safe, high-impact AI decisions?
options: Automatically approve outputs above a confidence threshold
Expose technical confidence scores without a review process
Use human review and a process to correct harmful errors
Assume a large model makes oversight unnecessary
why: Human oversight and correction mechanisms help detect and address harmful errors in high-impact decisions.

clues.why: Errors could seriously affect people.

hint: Choose safeguards proportional to the consequence of a mistake.
analysis: High-impact use calls for meaningful oversight and correction mechanisms. Automation alone cannot justify approving every output.
trap: A confident model can still make a harmful decision.
reasons: A confidence threshold alone does not provide adequate review for every high-impact use.
Scores alone do not create a meaningful path to review or correction.
Human oversight and correction mechanisms help detect and address harmful errors in high-impact decisions.
Model scale does not remove error, bias or accountability concerns.

q: An AI application should access only its required S3 objects. Apply which principle?
options: Make the bucket publicly readable for easier access
Encrypt the bucket but grant broad read permissions
Give the application a shared administrator credential
why: Least privilege restricts permitted actions and resources to those required for the application.

clues.why: Scope access to the actual task.

hint: Look for the smallest sufficient permission boundary.
analysis: The application needs specific objects, so permissions should be limited to those resources and necessary actions.
trap: An application needing access does not justify broad account permissions.
reasons: Public access exceeds the application’s need and may expose objects to others.
Least privilege restricts permitted actions and resources to those required for the application.
Encryption protects data but does not justify giving an application excess authorization.
Administrator credentials exceed the required scope and weaken accountability when shared.

q: Which AWS service records account API activity for auditing?
why: CloudTrail records supported account API events and related activity for audit and investigation.

clues.why: The requirement is an audit trail of account actions.

hint: Distinguish API auditing from model inference and text services.
analysis: The investigator needs records of supported account API events. Select the auditing service rather than language-processing capabilities.
trap: Logs serve different purposes; account activity is distinct from text generation.
reasons: Operational metrics are not a substitute for an account API activity audit trail.
Config tracks resource configuration; it does not replace the requested API event history.
CloudTrail records supported account API events and related activity for audit and investigation.
Artifact provides compliance documents rather than recording your account’s API calls.

q: Which service helps discover sensitive data in Amazon S3?
why: Macie helps discover sensitive data in S3 objects.

clues.why: The goal is identifying sensitive content in stored objects.

hint: Separate discovery of sensitive data from encryption of that data.
analysis: The combination of data discovery and S3 points to a purpose-built sensitive-data service. Discovery does not itself solve every protection requirement.
trap: Finding sensitive data is different from controlling who may read it.
reasons: Macie helps discover sensitive data in S3 objects.
KMS manages cryptographic keys; it does not perform the requested sensitive-content discovery.
CloudTrail records account activity, not a content classification scan of S3 objects.
IAM controls access permissions rather than discovering sensitive content.

q: A retrieved document tells an agent to reveal secrets. What is the main threat?
why: Prompt injection attempts to redirect an AI system through untrusted instructions, such as retrieved text.

clues.why: The instructions are arriving through untrusted source content.

hint: Ask whether source data is being promoted into authority.
analysis: A document is attempting to redirect the agent and expose secrets. Treat retrieved content as data and keep tool permissions outside its control.
trap: RAG grounding does not make retrieved instructions trustworthy.
reasons: The document is issuing hostile instructions rather than merely causing an unsupported factual statement.
Underfitting concerns inadequate learning and does not describe this instruction attack.
An output-length cap concerns generation size, not a request to reveal secrets.
Prompt injection attempts to redirect an AI system through untrusted instructions, such as retrieved text.

q: Which practice makes a training dataset’s origins traceable?
options: Store a model accuracy score without dataset metadata
Retain only the current dataset filename
Record the endpoint latency for each request
why: Lineage documents where the data came from and how it changed.

clues.why: The goal is documenting provenance and transformations.

hint: Look for the practice that lets an auditor follow the data’s history.
analysis: Traceability requires recording where data came from and how it changed. Access credentials do not provide that history.
trap: Logging everything without recording provenance may still leave the origin unclear.
reasons: Accuracy alone does not identify data origins or transformations.
Lineage documents where the data came from and how it changed.

Latency measures response time, not dataset provenance.

q: A retailer groups customers by similar purchasing behavior without predefined segment labels. Which technique fits?
why: Clustering discovers groups based on similarity without predefined target labels.

Clustering discovers groups based on similarity without predefined target labels.
Binary classification needs a defined two-class target rather than unknown segments.
Speech recognition transcribes audio and is unrelated to this grouping task.

clues.why: The groups are not known targets.

hint: Decide whether labels are given or groups must be discovered.
analysis: The desired output is customer groups, and no labels exist. This combines a grouping goal with unsupervised learning.

q: A spam filter raises false alarms on legitimate emails. Which metric directly asks how many predicted spam emails really are spam?
why: Precision measures actual positives among predicted positives, matching alert reliability.
reasons: Recall asks how many actual spam messages were found, not whether spam alerts are trustworthy.
Accuracy mixes correct spam and safe predictions and may hide the relevant error.
Precision measures actual positives among predicted positives, matching alert reliability.
Mean absolute error measures numeric prediction error, not class-alert reliability.

clues.why: The denominator is the set of positive predictions.

hint: Write out which group appears after the phrase out of.

trap: Precision and recall differ in their denominator, even when both discuss correct positives.

q: A classifier achieves excellent training results but performs poorly on unseen examples. What is the most likely issue?
why: Strong training results with poor unseen performance suggest fitting training-specific patterns that do not generalize.
reasons: Underfitting generally produces inadequate performance even on the training data.
Strong training results with poor unseen performance suggest fitting training-specific patterns that do not generalize.
Expected generalization would produce adequate results on unseen examples too.
Latency is response time and does not explain the described training-versus-test quality gap.

clues.why: Generalization, not training memorization, is the concern.

hint: Compare training performance with performance on new data.
analysis: A large training-versus-unseen performance gap suggests overfitting. Diagnose the gap rather than celebrating the training score.
trap: More training accuracy alone can worsen the actual problem.

q: Arrange this simplified ML workflow after the business problem is defined.
options: Train the model on the training split
Deploy the evaluated model and monitor it
Prepare the data and create appropriate dataset splits
Evaluate the trained model on held-out data
reasons: Training uses the prepared training data.
Deploy only after suitable evaluation, and keep monitoring.
Prepare data and separate evaluation data before training.

q: A website needs a prediction while a customer is waiting at checkout. Which inference pattern fits best?

Real-time inference serves low-latency predictions for interactive requests.

q: A team processes millions of records overnight and does not need immediate responses. Which inference pattern is most appropriate?
why: Batch inference suits large groups of predictions without an immediate-response requirement.

q: An on-demand model charges per input and output token. Which change most directly reduces generation cost when answer quality remains acceptable?

clues.why: The requirement is operational support, not only writing agent code.

analysis: Focus on deployment and operations for agents. AgentCore is designed for that role, whereas specialized language services are not a general runtime.

q: A company wants an assistant that helps develop software from specifications. Which AWS tool best fits?

reasons: Transcribe converts speech recordings to text.

Kiro is an AI development tool supporting specification-driven software development.

clues.why: The application is software development, not speech processing.

hint: Identify the business workflow before selecting the tool.
analysis: The request concerns moving specifications into software development work. Choose the development tool rather than a specialized text/audio service.
trap: AI-related names alone do not establish a match to the workflow.

q: Two models meet quality requirements. One is faster and cheaper for the company’s representative workload. What is the best next selection step?
options: Benchmark the tradeoffs and choose the workload-appropriate model
why: Representative testing lets the team compare quality, latency and cost against requirements.
reasons: Size alone does not show suitability once quality requirements are met.
Representative testing lets the team compare quality, latency and cost against requirements.
Popularity is not evidence that the model meets this workload’s constraints.
Measured latency and cost are directly relevant selection criteria.

clues.why: Evaluate the actual use case rather than a generic ranking.

hint: Look for a decision grounded in requirements and measured tradeoffs.
analysis: Both candidates pass the quality threshold. Compare cost and responsiveness under realistic conditions before choosing.
trap: The largest or most famous model is not automatically the best business fit.

q: Which TWO approaches can supply task guidance or current document information without changing model weights?
options: Retrieve relevant source passages with RAG
Fine-tune the model on domain examples
Include a few demonstrations in the prompt
Train a student model by distillation
reasons: RAG supplies runtime source context without itself changing model weights.
Fine-tuning updates model parameters.
Few-shot demonstrations guide the inference call through prompt context.
Pre-training learns model parameters from data.
Distillation trains a student and changes the student model’s parameters.
why: RAG and few-shot prompting can modify runtime context without training the model.

clues.why: Separate runtime context from training-based parameter changes.

hint: Choose exactly two options that act through the model’s input context.
analysis: Retrieval and prompt demonstrations modify the information provided at inference time. Training, fine-tuning and distillation learn parameters.
trap: Both RAG and prompting avoid weight updates, but they meet different information needs.

q: A model must label sentiment from an instruction with no demonstrations in the prompt. Which prompting technique is this?
why: Zero-shot asks the model to perform the task without demonstrations.
reasons: Few-shot includes a small set of demonstrations.
Zero-shot asks the model to perform the task without demonstrations.
Distillation trains a student from a teacher.
Continuous pre-training changes model parameters with additional training.

clues.why: Count examples rather than instructions.

hint: An instruction is not the same thing as a worked example.
analysis: The task and output can be specified in detail while still being zero-shot if no demonstrations are supplied.
trap: Zero-shot does not mean the prompt contains no guidance.

q: An application needs semantic search over internal documents. What should be compared to find related meaning?
why: Embedding-vector similarity can help compare meaning between queries and documents.
reasons: Exact filenames can miss semantically related material with different wording.
Encryption keys serve security needs and are not semantic feature vectors.
Embedding-vector similarity can help compare meaning between queries and documents.
Creation time describes recency, not semantic similarity.

clues.why: The goal is similarity of meaning, not exact filename matching.

hint: Choose a representation designed for comparing semantic features.
analysis: Meaning-based retrieval commonly compares query and content embeddings. Retrieval quality still depends on the model and indexing strategy.
trap: Semantic similarity is useful evidence of relevance, not a guarantee of factual accuracy.

q: Why might a RAG pipeline split long source documents into chunks?
options: To retrieve focused passages that fit the available context
why: Focused chunks can improve passage retrieval and fit within input constraints.

Focused chunks can improve passage retrieval and fit within input constraints.
Access controls remain necessary regardless of chunk size.

hint: Think about what the retriever returns and the model can accept.
analysis: Chunking creates units suitable for retrieval and context assembly. Chunk size should preserve enough surrounding meaning for the task.
trap: Smaller chunks are not always better; too little context can break meaning.

q: A RAG chatbot cites a policy paragraph that was replaced last month. What should the team investigate first?
options: Check source freshness and index synchronization
Switch to a larger model without checking the retrieved context
why: Check source versions, ingestion and index updates to determine why obsolete information was retrieved.
reasons: Temperature changes sampling behavior and does not refresh outdated documents.
Check source versions, ingestion and index updates to determine why obsolete information was retrieved.
Longer output can still repeat the same obsolete passage.
A larger model can receive and rely on the same stale context; inspect retrieval first.

clues.why: The content used for grounding is outdated.

hint: Trace the answer back to the source and its ingestion process.
analysis: The visible failure is stale grounding material. Check source versions, refresh processes and retrieval results before changing the model.
trap: A citation proves a source was referenced, not that the source is current.

q: A prompt asks for a JSON object with three named fields. What most directly improves the chance of the desired format?
options: Describe only the topic and omit the field names
Specify the required schema and a valid example, then validate output
Use a higher temperature to encourage format variation
Repeat an ambiguous request several times without testing
why: Clear structure and a valid example improve guidance; programmatic validation still checks whether the response meets the contract.
reasons: Omitting field names leaves the required output structure ambiguous.
Clear structure and a valid example improve guidance; programmatic validation still checks whether the response meets the contract.
More variation does not directly improve adherence to an exact JSON structure.
Repeating ambiguity does not resolve it or verify valid JSON.

clues.why: The desired structure should be explicit.

hint: Choose the change that removes ambiguity from the requested output.
analysis: Specify fields, constraints and an example. Validate the response programmatically because prompting alone does not guarantee valid JSON.
trap: A well-written format instruction still needs output validation in production.

q: A model response must stop after a short answer. Which inference setting most directly limits generated length?
why: Maximum output tokens directly caps generation length, although a cap can truncate content.
reasons: Maximum output tokens directly caps generation length, although a cap can truncate content.
Temperature influences sampling variation, not a hard length cap.

Examples can guide behavior but do not enforce a hard output-length limit.

clues.why: The control should act on output tokens.

hint: Separate inference settings from training and infrastructure settings.
analysis: The requirement is a length cap. Use the output-token limit and check that the resulting answer is complete enough.
trap: Truncating an answer is not the same as teaching the model to be concise.

q: Match each foundation-model evaluation technique to what it assesses.
reasons: BERTScore uses contextual embeddings to compare generated and reference text.

why: BLEU is associated with translation overlap; ROUGE with summary overlap; BERTScore with semantic comparison; an LLM judge with rubric-based model assessment.

clues.why: Distinguish reference overlap, semantic similarity and model-based judgment.

hint: Identify how each metric compares or judges the generated response.
analysis: Different techniques capture different aspects of text quality. None of these alone guarantees factual correctness.
trap: A good overlap score does not prove truth; a model judge also needs validation.
prompts: Translation comparison using n-gram precision and a brevity penalty
A language model scores answers against a rubric

q: A summarization team wants an overlap-based metric comparing generated summaries with reference summaries. Which fits?
why: ROUGE compares overlap with reference text and is commonly used for summary evaluation.
reasons: ROUGE compares overlap with reference text and is commonly used for summary evaluation.

Task completion is a business outcome measure rather than a reference-overlap metric.
Throughput measures processing volume or speed, not textual summary overlap.

clues.why: A reference-text comparison is requested.

hint: Separate content-quality measures from system-operation measures.
analysis: The requirement is summary overlap, which points to ROUGE. Add checks for factuality because overlap alone does not establish truth.
trap: A summary can share many words with a reference and still contain factual errors.

q: A company uses another language model to score generated answers. What is an important evaluation risk?
options: The judge can have its own biases and errors
The candidate model no longer needs prompts
why: Model judges can be biased or mistaken; calibrate them against suitable criteria and human judgments.
reasons: Model judges can be biased or mistaken; calibrate them against suitable criteria and human judgments.
A second model is not an infallible source of truth.
Human review remains possible and can help validate the evaluation.
A judge does not eliminate the candidate model’s input requirements.

clues.why: The evaluator is itself a fallible model.

hint: Apply the same skepticism to the evaluator as to the system being evaluated.
analysis: LLM-as-a-judge can scale assessment but requires validation. Compare judgments against trusted examples and inspect disagreement.
trap: Automating an evaluation does not remove subjectivity or error.

q: A support agent retrieves correct documents but frequently fails to complete refund tasks. What should its evaluation include?

analysis: Correct retrieval is necessary but insufficient for a tool-using agent. Assess completion, failures and safe handling of actions.

q: A team repeatedly changes prompts and cannot tell which version caused a quality regression. What practice helps?

q: A team wants one place to document a model’s intended use, limitations and evaluation results. What fits?

q: A region is almost absent from training data but is part of the intended user population. Which TWO actions best investigate this risk?
options: Evaluate results separately for users from that region
Assume the overall accuracy establishes regional fairness
Collect or curate suitable examples representing that population
Increase hosting capacity instead of evaluating the regional data
Exclude regional failures from the evaluation report
reasons: Subgroup evaluation helps identify failures hidden by aggregate results.

q: A team selects an AI model for routine tasks that a smaller model can handle at the required quality. Which choice supports sustainability?

Choosing a fit-for-purpose model and measuring resource use can reduce unnecessary computation.

Understandable reasons and human review support accountability and correction.

q: A model accesses customer data through a managed AWS service. Which statement best reflects shared responsibility?

Customer responsibilities include appropriate data handling and access controls; exact duties vary by service.

q: An agent may read order status but must never issue refunds. Which TWO controls directly enforce this action boundary?
options: Grant the agent identity only the required order-read permissions
Tell the model in its system prompt that refunds are forbidden
Expose only approved read-only tools and reject unauthorized actions at execution
Hide the refund button while keeping a broad refund-capable API credential
Lower the model temperature to zero
reasons: Scoped identity permissions limit the operations the agent can actually perform.
A prompt supports behavior but is not an authorization boundary.
Execution-time tool restrictions can block actions outside the approved capability set.
Hiding a UI element does not revoke the underlying credential’s capabilities.

clues.why: The control must block the prohibited action outside model-generated instructions.

hint: Select the controls enforced by identity and tool execution, not wording or sampling.
analysis: Use least-privilege authorization and an approved tool-execution boundary together. Prompt instructions can complement these controls but cannot replace them.
